newsitem.title: ITALY: Mediobanca's Cuccia seen behind Marzotto deal.
newsitem.headline: Mediobanca's Cuccia seen behind Marzotto deal.

text.p: The merger of Italian industrial conglomerate HPI with textiles group Marzotto is widely believed to have been the handiwork of the grand old man of Italian finance, Enrico Cuccia.

"I don't know if this deal is going to increase the competitiveness of the two groups involved but it looks like another Cuccia masterpiece," said one Milan-based equities analyst on Sunday who asked not to be identified.

The newly-created HPI, which stands for Holding di Partecipazioni Industriali, and Marzotto jointly unveiled plans on Friday night to merge their operations and create one of the biggest textiles and clothing groups in the world.
The new entity, to be called Gruppo Industriale Marzotto, will also own Italy's second largest publishing group, Rizzoli Corriere della Sera (RCS).

Milan's financial community got wind that a major deal was afoot on Friday after shares in Gemina, a financial holding company, were suspended from trading on the bourse. HPI, which is due to start trading on the stock exchange on Monday, was formed by spinning off Gemina's industrial interests.

Behind the latest upheaval in Italian finance is the guiding hand of Mediobanca, the secretive Milan merchant bank still dominated by Enrico Cuccia, a 90-year-old Sicilian who is the bank's honorary chairman.
Pietro Marzotto, who will chair the new group, said he was first sounded out last year about the merger idea by Mediobanca.
"I was called by Mediobanca. The project has been under study since last July and an agreement was reached in January," Marzotto told a news conference on Saturday.

The HPI-Marzotto merger is the latest in a sequence of events following the collapse of the so-called "SuperGemina" deal -- a plan hatched by Cuccia to bundle Gemina's interests with the former Ferruzzi agri-chemicals empire.
After the deal was abandoned, following the discovery of huge losses at RCS, Ferruzzi was renamed Compart and Gemina's core interests hived off into HPI.
"SuperGemina is dead and buried but the idea is still to have something big and to put everything into it," said one Milan stockbroker.

Marzotto staunchly defended the deal saying its logic was primarily industrial. "With this merger we have not created a financial group but a large industrial group, two thirds in textiles and one third in publishing."
The proposed managing director is HPI board member Maurizio Romiti, son of carmaker Fiat head Cesare Romiti.
The groups have already worked out a proposed share swap ratio of 13 ordinary HPI shares for one ordinary Marzotto share and eight HPI savings shares for one Marzotto savings share.

Marzotto shares closed down 190 lire at 13,450 on the Milan stock market on Friday, shortly before it announced a consolidated net profit for 1996 of 58.1 billion lire, up from 50.1 billion in 1995, and a turnover of 2.225 trillion lire.
HPI's spin-off from Gemina has meant the transfer to HPI of editorial unit RCS Editori and textile groups Fila and GFT.

The new company will have a portfolio of significant stakes in various Italian companies, including 20.9 percent in paper group Cartiere Burgo, 25 percent of household furnishings company Zucchi and one percent or less stakes in Credito Italiano, Banca Commerciale Italiana and Mediobanca.
